paragraphs.text:
A load is an applied force, such as a push or pull.
Deformation is a change in size or shape.

Elasticity means that a material comes back toward its old size and shape after the load is removed.
Many solids can recover approximately when the conditions allow it.

Recovery needs a suitable temperature and suitable loading conditions, including how the force is applied.
The deformation must be small enough for that material, without damage or a significant irreversible change.
An irreversible change does not undo itself when the force is removed.

Small deformation alone does not guarantee complete recovery.
Stress is the internal force per unit area: the force carried by each equal-sized part of an area inside the material.
Recovery also depends on this stress.

Material state means its condition and how it has been prepared.
Observation time means how long we watch after removing the load.
The material's state and this watching time also affect the recovery we observe.

Plastic deformation is a change in size or shape that remains after the load is removed.
Many materials can change this way under some conditions.
Elasticity and plasticity describe whether a material's change recovers or lasts.

Different materials respond differently to forces.
Rubber and some kinds of steel can show clear elastic behavior, but only within their own conditions and deformation ranges.

Tension means pulling to stretch a material.
Relative elongation, also called tensile strain, is the added length divided by the original length.
Strain tells us what fraction of the starting length the stretch adds.

The Greek letter epsilon names this strain.
The original textbook gives steel that still obeys Hooke's law at $\varepsilon=1\%$ as an example.
The percentage shown means one part of added length for every hundred parts of original length.

Hooke's law says that stress is proportional to strain within the linear elastic range.
Proportional means that doubling the stress doubles the strain while the material stays within that range.
Linear means the stress-versus-strain graph is a straight line in that range.

The textbook's steel example is not a shared upper limit of linear elasticity for all steels.
Steel behavior depends on the particular material and conditions.

The textbook also gives an example of rubber remaining elastic when $\varepsilon$ reaches several tens of percent.
Rubber may return toward its old shape without obeying the doubling rule.
This is nonlinear elasticity: recovery without the same straight-line relation between stress and strain.

This lesson uses "elastic materials" to mean materials whose deformation can recover under suitable conditions.
The name does not promise the same doubling rule throughout every deformation range.

The original textbook uses wet clay, plastics, and lead as examples of materials that readily keep a changed shape.
Under the conditions it describes, their elastic range may be small.
Even a modest load may then leave permanent deformation.

The textbook calls these examples "plastic materials" because their deformation lasts after the load is removed.
Plastic deformation does not simply mean being made of everyday plastic.
It can happen in other materials too.

The name does not mean that all plastics or all lead always behave this way.
Temperature and composition, meaning what the material is made of, can change its response.

Loading rate means how quickly the force is applied.
Load duration means how long the force stays applied.
Both can change whether deformation recovers or lasts.

A time-dependent response is a change that depends on how long a load acts or how long recovery is watched.
The same material may respond differently if these times or the other conditions change.

The distinction between elastic and plastic behavior depends on conditions.
The same material can respond differently at different stresses, temperatures, and loading conditions.

Steel can change elastically under smaller loads when conditions allow.
At its yield conditions, permanent deformation begins.
These conditions depend on the steel and how the force is applied.

A press is an industrial machine that squeezes metal.
It applies high pressure to steel parts so that they deform plastically and keep their new shape.
This is a description of industrial shaping, not an activity to try.

Different steel parts can start to deform permanently under different conditions.
A single stress value cannot mark the same elastic-to-plastic boundary for all steels.

Temperature affects how a material responds to forces.
Hot working means shaping metal while it is hot.
To forge metal means to shape it by hammering or pressing.

Under suitable hot-working conditions, steel or iron is usually easier to forge than when cold.
Even hot metal has limits on how much it can deform.

Forging is industrial work, not an activity to try here.
The lead-cooling example below also describes material behavior, not an experiment to perform.

The original textbook gives cooling lead below $-100^\circ C$ as an example.
Lead that readily deforms plastically at room temperature can show clearer elastic behavior at lower temperatures.

The printed temperature is the textbook's illustration, not an exact changeover point for all lead materials.
Low temperature does not guarantee that every load causes only elastic deformation.

Fracture means breaking.
Brittleness describes breaking after very little plastic deformation.
Plastic deformation is a lasting size or shape change after the force is removed.

A specimen is a test piece of a material.
In this lesson's cast iron example, the test piece breaks after only a small total stretch.
The steel test piece described later stretches much more before breaking.

Glass objects and porcelain often show clear brittle behavior.
They may break on impact with a hard floor even after falling from a modest height.

The original textbook also lists cast iron, marble, and amber as brittle examples.
Plasticity means the ability to keep a changed shape after the force is removed.
That change may be stretching, bending, squeezing, or another shape change.

Ductility means the ability to stretch permanently before breaking when pulled in tension.
Under the material states and loading conditions usually discussed, steel, copper, and lead often show greater plasticity or ductility than the brittle examples.

The comparison depends on temperature, the material's preparation, and how it is loaded.
Steel, copper, and lead can also break in a brittle way under other conditions.

The graphs compare test pieces pulled in tension, meaning pulled to stretch.
They compare brittle breaking with breaking after a large permanent stretch.

The original cross-sectional area measures how much flat surface there is straight across the test piece before stretching.
For a round test piece, picture the whole circle at its end, not just the distance across it.
Engineering stress is the pulling force divided by that original area.

The original gauge length is the starting distance between the points used to measure stretch.
Engineering strain is the added length divided by that original distance.

The graphs plot tensile stress $\sigma$ against relative elongation $\varepsilon$.
Figures 89 and 90 show the textbook's cast iron and steel test pieces, in that order.
The comparison uses engineering stress and engineering strain.

Necking means that the test piece becomes narrower in a small local region as it stretches.
Local true stress uses the current area straight across that region, not the original area.
Do not confuse local true stress with engineering stress or replace the original gauge length with a changing local length.

Warning: the textbook's numerical dataset and curves are UNRECONCILED and NOT verified material constants.
The printed numbers and curves have not been shown to agree, and they are not confirmed, dependable values for a material.
They are kept only to compare kinds of behavior, not to calculate reliable material properties.

The stress unit below means newtons of force per square metre of area.
In the printed example, cast iron elongates by 0.1%, and its stress is approximately $8\times10^7$ N/m$^2$.
At the same relative elongation, the printed steel stress is $2\times10^7$ N/m$^2$.

Do not combine these data with the previous lesson's Young's modulus example to calculate material properties.
Young's modulus describes stiffness in linear elastic tension: how strongly a material resists stretching within its straight-line elastic range.
These unresolved data cannot give verified stiffness, strength, or other material values.

Ultimate tensile strength means the maximum engineering stress reached while a test piece is pulled.
According to the textbook, cast iron breaks at an elongation of 0.45%, with almost no clear stage of permanent stretching.
Its printed ultimate tensile strength is $12\times10^7$ N/m$^2$.

That maximum engineering stress is not the local true stress at the place where the test piece breaks.
The scale near the curve's endpoint is only an approximate picture.
Do not read the endpoint as an exact value matching the breaking value stated in the text.

The textbook's steel test piece remains elastic at $\varepsilon=0.45\%$ and breaks only at $\varepsilon\approx15\%$.
Its printed ultimate tensile strength is $7\times10^8$ N/m$^2$.
This steel example breaks after a much larger total stretch than the cast iron example.

The elastic ranges, breaking stretches, and strengths depend on the particular test piece and test conditions.
Do not combine this steel example with the earlier steel range to make a limit for all steels.

The cast iron graph emphasizes almost no clear stage of permanent stretching before breaking.
Other brittle materials may also break with little noticeable plastic deformation.
This does not mean that all brittle materials resist stretching equally.

Stiffness means resistance to a change in size or shape.
Within the linear elastic range, a steeper stress-versus-strain curve means a larger stress increase for the same small increase in strain.
The comparison must use the same kind of tensile test, because stiffness and test conditions affect the curve.

Brittleness concerns how little permanent deformation happens before breaking, not how steep the graph is.
Brittle materials do not all have curves of the same steepness.
These unresolved curves must not be used to calculate reliable numerical slopes.

The phrase "almost no plastic deformation" is an approximate way to compare brittle and ductile behavior here.
It does not mean that every brittle material has absolutely no lasting deformation under every condition.
